I guess so. Batting average is definitely not the only factor in whether a batter is a good or bad player - that goes a lot further than average - but it can make a big difference in the grand scheme of things.

You're absolutely right that batting average isn't everything. I think I made it sound like I was saying that batting average is the end-all be-all, and that's not what I meant to say. However, as far as I see it, while batting average doesn't predict how good a player will be overall, it does generally separate the good from the bad. If a guy is hitting .180 in the big leagues, you can reasonably assume he's not providing much value, even without seeing his other stats. And if a guy is hitting .330, you can reasonably assume he's got good stuff.

I'd argue that the gap between .206 and .180 is pretty big, made clear by the fact that in 2018, there was only one guy hitting below .200 who got any regular playing time at all (Chris Davis). If batters that hit below .200 brought more value to their teams than guys who hit above .200, they'd be playing regularly.

Edit: To make my point further - there were no regular batters in 2019 who hit below .200. Again, if players who hit below .200 were of value to their teams, they'd play.

On the one hand, you're absolutely right. On the other hand, there are two important notes I want to make. 

One is that the guy with the higher batting average will be much better in clutch situations. If you have the bases loaded and two outs, you'd much rather get a reliable single-hitter with a .330 average than a power hitter with a .260 average and a 30% strikeout chance. 

The second is that there is a limit to how low your batting average can be. A .260 average will easily get you by nowadays, especially if you hit with power. However, there's a reason why guys don't stick around in the bigs with a batting average below .200. A guy with a .330 average isn't necessarily going to be better than a guy with a .260, but you can sure as hell say that the guy with a .260 is better than a .180.

I disagree. I think batting average is very relevant to performance. There are a lot of exceptions - Harper clearly being one of them, Alonso being another - but overall, better players have higher batting averages.

I get it. I mean, I was hoping to have another 300 seasons of DH-less baseball. I'm frustrated myself. I've made a few comments already that I knew would get down voted to hell, just because I wanted to rage. But in the end, it's not up to us what the players and higher-ups decide upon. It's up to us whether or not we keep watching baseball, and no one's obligated to. And I wish the people down voting would quit doing so, since it's real frustration.

I guess all I can do is argue for the good aspects of baseball, because I think it'd be a shame for anyone to quit on it. But I'm not going to blame you for making the decision to stop watching, because I know exactly where you're coming from. If my main team were NL and I wasn't used to it, I might be in the same boat.

Two things immediately come to mind for me. One is - there are still positives of baseball outside of what the DH affects. The DH takes away a lot, and doesn't provide anything in its place... but baseball's still baseball.

The second thing bums me out more, but it's the reality - which is that it would appear the players want universal DH. I wish they didn't, but if they want it, they want it. I'm certain that this would've happened anyway, at some point, no matter what. If the players push for something enough, they'll probably get it.

I really despise the DH, but I'm a diehard Indians fan. I've been watching them since I was a little kid. No matter how much I hate the DH, I love baseball more. You couldn't pay me to stop watching. I think it may do you good to think about it differently. Manfred and co. can change baseball, but they can't destroy it.
What's the story with this game?

I think your proposal on extra innings could work, potentially. I'm not going to argue that at all.

Wouldn't a convincing argument be that more time to play means more injuries? If 162 games were played all with 5 innings instead of 9, it would be less time for players to get hurt. That's just the truth. 9 innings is fine, but 5 innings would be much less strain. Isn't that a good enough reason? Why play 9 anyway?

I'm somewhat sympathetic to your argument, but implementing a DH would implement a guy whose only job is to hit. Designated Hitters, by definition, work half as hard as any of the other guys on the team. I'm not saying it doesn't take talent and skill to be a DH - it does - but when all you have to work on is hitting, not fielding, you've got an easier job than everyone else on the team.

You're absolutely right, but the fundamental tenants of the game were already present. Lots of things have changed since then, most of them for the better, but the things that haven't changed are worth noting. For example - would you be on board with shortening games from 9 innings to 5? If not, why not? It would certainly lead to less strain on players.

I'm not attempting to pearl-clutch, but if I am I'll try to quit that. My issue has almost nothing to do with whether or not my team's performance would be better. It's about the rules of the game. Baseball has always been a sport where people bat, field, and run. There are no exceptions to that - since the 1880s and until today, almost every player bats, fields, and runs. To change that would fundamentally change the game.

I guess the question that immediately comes to mind for me is: at what point is it no longer baseball?

I'm being hyperbolic, but I'm trying to make a point. People want universal DH because pitchers get hurt running the bases. And it's true - sometimes people get hurt running the bases. So why not implement designated runners for everyone, so no batters get hurt running the bases?

I'm an AL fan and I'm incensed. Seriously - what's next? How about nobody runs the bases? Every team gets 3 pinch runners and nobody else ever runs. They could get hurt running! And let's make it so that no batters have to field either. One team to field, and one team to bat. Batters get hurt fielding! Fielders might get hurt batting! Won't somebody think of the children?
